44171910.extract:
The Morris Park Aerodrome, established in 1908, is a significant landmark in the history of aviation. It was the first officially established airfield in the United States, located in what is now the Morris Park section of the Bronx, New York. The aerodrome, occupying the grounds of the former Morris Park Racecourse, was in operation for only two years before the land was developed for residential use. Despite its short lifespan, the aerodrome played a crucial role in early aviation history, hosting the first exhibition of aircraft in the United States.

The Morris Park Aerodrome, in operation from 1908 to 1909, was the first flying field in the United States. The aerodrome served as the site of the first exhibition of aircraft in the United States, hosting a number of notable events and demonstrations. The aerodrome was a focal point for early aviation enthusiasts and played a significant role in the development of aviation in the United States.

Today, the site of the Morris Park Aerodrome is no longer in use as an airfield. However, efforts are being made to honor the aerodrome's aviation history. An archivist at Fordham Prep has tracked down evidence of the aerodrome's significance, and there are plans to commemorate its legacy in the Morris Park neighborhood.

The **Morris Park Aerodrome** was a short-lived [airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airfield "Airfield") in what is now the [Morris Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park,_Bronx "Morris Park, Bronx") section of [the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx "The Bronx"), New York, United States. The [aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodrome "Aerodrome"), which was in operation from 1908 to 1909, was the first flying field in the nation, occupying the grounds of the former [Morris Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse "Morris Park Racecourse"). The [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York"), after a split from the [Aero Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_of_America "Aero Club of America"), leased the land in 1908 and used it as an aerodrome for two years until it was developed for residential use.

The Society used the grounds for building and testing aircraft, and for putting on public exhibitions including major events in November 1908, and June 1909. The former, captured in an oil painting by [Rudolph Dirks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Dirks "Rudolph Dirks") titled _The Fledglings_, included several glider flights by sixteen-year-old [Laurence Lesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_J._Lesh "Laurence J. Lesh"), culminating in a crash in which he was severely injured. The latter had flights by [Glenn Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Curtiss "Glenn Curtiss") in his _[Golden Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss\_No.\_1 "Curtiss No. 1")_ motorized biplane, including the first demonstration of a stable flight around a closed course using [ailerons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aileron "Aileron") for lateral control. The exhibitions also featured [balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balloon_(aeronautics) "Balloon (aeronautics)"), [kites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kite "Kite"), [helicopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicopter "Helicopter"), parachute jumps, and ground vehicles driven by propellers known as wind wagons.

Other projects worked on during the two years of operation included a biplane by Wilbur Kimball using eight propellors and a novel [rudder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudder "Rudder") system for lateral control, and a biplane from Frederick Schneider with three adjustable-pitch [propellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propeller "Propeller"). Stanley Beach and Charles Willard constructed what is believed to be the first [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") flown in the United States. Joel T. Rice demonstrated a 100-foot (30 m) long dirigible using [vectored thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring"), capable of carrying 15 passengers.

The aerodrome ceased operations at the end of 1909, when the land was given over to residential development. The Society moved its operations to a larger facility on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), which would eventually become known as [Roosevelt Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)").

> "What the Society needed in the way of ground was not very easy to find. Free, open space over which to fly was not alone sufficient. It was equally, if not, indeed, still more necessary, that the grounds should be close to the city. For it was the ambition of the Society to have its grounds so near at hand that the distance should place no obstacle in the way even of the poorest inventor who wanted to run out to the workshops and devote his spare hours to the material realization of his ideas."

Edward T. Tandy, An Epitome of the Work of The Aeronautic Society from July, 1908, to December, 1909

In 1905, the [Aero Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aero_Club_of_America "Aero Club of America"), patterned after the [Aero Club of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A%C3%A9ro-Club_de_France "Aéro-Club de France"), was formed as an offshoot of the [Automobile Club of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile_Club_of_America "Automobile Club of America"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-1) Three years later, in response to sentiment that the aero club should be more active, president [Cortlandt Field Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cortlandt_F._Bishop "Cortlandt F. Bishop") appointed a Committee of Aviation, chaired by [Albert Triaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_C._Triaca "Albert C. Triaca"), to promote more work on aeroplanes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2) The Committee, however, was unable to make any progress; Society chronicler Edward T. Tandy later wrote, "they found their efforts smothered by a cold, wet blanket of official objection. When they attempted to persevere, they were promptly stopped. The power that ruled that organization did not believe in aviation ... The doing of anything practical was not to be attempted."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 7–8

Unsatisfied with the progress being made by the committee, fifty members of the club split off on June 10, 1908, forming the [Aeronautical Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautical_Society_of_New_York "Aeronautical Society of New York"). Initial membership included Lee Burridge, Albert Triaca, [Willard Kimball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ravel_Kimball "Wilbur Ravel Kimball"), Roger Whitman, [William Hammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Joseph_Hammer "William Joseph Hammer"), [Leo Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Leo_Stevens "Albert Leo Stevens"), Daniel Brine, and [Stanley Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Yale_Beach "Stanley Yale Beach").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2) Burridge (who would later be President of the Society[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-4)) spoke of plans to acquire an airfield: "this society is going to stand for something tangible, practical, and it proposes to secure experimental grounds as soon as possible where men who have been working on problems of aeronautics will be enabled to try out their machines".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908b-2)

That summer, the Society looked at several properties from [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") to [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island") and ultimately identified the grounds of the old [Morris Park Racecourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Racecourse "Morris Park Racecourse") as the best location.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:8-5) The racecourse had closed in 1904, after which the 372-acre (151 ha) property was used for [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_racing "Auto racing") and [motorcycle racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorcycle_racing "Motorcycle racing") for a few years. It was convenient to the recently opened [West Farms Square subway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Farms_Square%E2%80%93East_Tremont_Avenue_station "West Farms Square–East Tremont Avenue station") and a trolley stop, as well as a range of cafes and residences which could be had for inexpensive rents. Proximity to public transportation was considered essential, making the field accessible to all experimenters, not just the affluent.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 273–274

[![Image 3: Color picture postcard showing a three-story building in a wooded setting. Printed under the photo is "Woodmansten Inn, Pelham Parkway and Williamsbridge Road, Westchester, N.Y."](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_%28front%29.webp/250px-Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_%28front%29.webp.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Woodmansten_Inn_Postcard_(front).webp)

The Woodmansten Inn

The location provided open spaces on a level elevation, several existing buildings which could be repurposed as workshops, and a larger building with a neatly trimmed lawn and flower beds to use as a clubhouse.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:9-7) The nearby Woodmansten Inn, built in 1902, had a restaurant and sleeping facilities.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:13-8) An advertisement in the 1908 exhibition program offered dinner with wine for $3.00 (equivalent to $74 in 2024)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:18-9): 4  and Tandy described it as "one of the best and most fashionable hotels of the city".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 9

Morris Park Aerodrome (occasionally called the Morris Park Volery[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909a-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:24-11)) was made available to members for the first time on the weekend of August 29 and 30, 1908.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 274  A lease was signed on or about August 31,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:8-5) running until December 31, 1909,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:3-12) although it was already known that the land was eventually destined for residential development.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 9  By the next week, fences adjacent to the track were being removed to provide a clear straight path of at least 0.62 miles (1.00 km), locations were being considered for constructing a machine shop, and plans were being made for an exhibition where "Freak machines will have a chance to show what they can do as well as the more orthodox types."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:3-12)

[![Image 4: Photograph of an ornate five-story building with multiple setbacks, balconies, and awnings.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_%281898%29_%2817975359990%29.jpg/250px-The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_%281898%29_%2817975359990%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_American_turf-_an_historical_account_of_racing_in_the_United_States_-_with_biographical_sketches_of_turf_celebrities._1898_(1898)_(17975359990).jpg)

Morris Park Clubhouse in 1898

Morris Park was the first flying field in the United States[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-13) although by the end of 1909, _[All the World's Air-Ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janes\_All\_the\_World%27s\_Aircraft "Janes All the World's Aircraft")_ by [Fred Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_T._Jane "Fred T. Jane") listed it as one of eight such facilities in the country.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-14) The primary purpose of the field was the construction of aircraft, although it was also used for flight instruction, hosting Albert Tiiaca's International School of Aeronautics.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:9-7) Within the first 12 months of operation, 24 full-sized heavier-than-air airplanes were constructed on the field, plus an assortment of gliders, airships, and a large number of scale models. Almost 25% of the Society membership held aircraft patents or were directly involved in the construction of aircraft at the field.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 6

Lacking any hill high enough to launch a glider from, the Society built two facilities for assisting in glider launches. The first was a catapult. The second was a larger structure of wooden construction, which was erected without first obtaining a building permit. After a glider spent an entire day atop the structure waiting for winds favorable for launching, city officials declared that the structure was a residence, and since it lacked both plumbing and a fire escape, condemned it, compelling it to be torn down.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 14

Many of the aircraft built at Morris Park were failures, with aviation historians taking a pessimistic view of the members' skills. [Preston Bassett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preston_Bassett "Preston Bassett") described the Aeronautic Society as "a group of enthusiastic young men in New York City, all with plans for building their own machines [whose] enthusiasm far outran their ability to perform".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:24-11) Paul Glenshaw, wrote "The group could boast of few successes. Descriptions of the members’ experiments included words like 'tree' and 'fence', coupled with 'plunged' and 'smashed'."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-15)

On October 18, the first exhibition of the Society was announced for November 3 to coincide with [election day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_United_States_presidential_election "1908 United States presidential election"). There were plans for two airplanes from the [Aerial Experiment Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_Experiment_Association "Aerial Experiment Association")_([June Bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA\_June\_Bug "AEA June Bug")_ and _[Silver Dart)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AEA\_Silver\_Dart "AEA Silver Dart")_ to compete, a five-mile [dirigible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship") race, [kites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kite "Kite"), and [gliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glider_(aircraft) "Glider (aircraft)"); the kite contest was open to [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_school "Primary school") students with no entry fee.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16) There were also plans for one-, five-, and ten-mile [motorcycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorcycle "Motorcycle") races sponsored by the [Federation of American Motorcyclists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Motorcyclist_Association "American Motorcyclist Association")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 269  and for the [U.S. Weather Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") to demonstrate the use of kites and captive balloons to collect atmospheric data.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 277 [Lillian Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._Lilian_Todd "E. Lilian Todd"), the only female member of the Society,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-17) was expected to show a "large model airplane" of her own design.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:18-9): 11

Admission to the exhibition was $0.50 (equivalent to $17.5 in 2024), with the [subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway "New York City Subway") ride from [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") taking 40 minutes.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 269  An estimated 20,000 spectators showed up, far exceeding expectations. Although several hundred people had volunteered to act as marshals (equipped with badges and sticks), a large number of people swarmed past the gate with only about 3,500 people having paid their admission fee.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Crouch_2011-6): 279  Tandy wrote that in the years since the race track had been in use, the fences had deteriorated and that "The payment for admission proved a matter of almost quixotic courtesy."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 15

[![Image 5: A man hangs below a glider in flight. Many people (at least 100) are watching.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png/250px-Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lawrence_J._Lesh_in_Glider_Flight_at_Morris_Park.png)

Lesh in the air at the 1908 exhibition

Sixteen-year-old glider pilot [Laurence J. Lesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_J._Lesh "Laurence J. Lesh") was the highlight of the exhibition. A protégé of aviation pioneer [Octave Chanute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Chanute "Octave Chanute"), Lesh was the first known aviator in Canada, having built and flown horse-drawn gliders as early as 1907 when he was fourteen years old. He became known for a record-setting 24 minute, 6.2-mile (10.0 km) flight towed by a motor boat on the [St. Lawrence River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Lawrence_River "St. Lawrence River").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:0-18)

Lesh [broke his ankle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankle_fracture "Ankle fracture") when he crashed during his third flight of the day after reaching a maximum altitude of 70 feet (21 m) and travelling about 200 feet (61 m).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908a-19) One account attributed the cause of the crash to inexperience flying this model of glider which lacked the rudder used on his earlier designs.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:10-20) Another account blamed the crowd which got in his way while attempting to land.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:17-3): 17  In any case, the injuries sustained in the crash sent Lesh to the hospital and took a year of [rehabilitative therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_therapy "Physical therapy") to fully recover.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:0-18)

The glider had been launched by rope tow behind [a 1907 Thomas Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Motor_Company#New_York_to_Paris_Race "Thomas Motor Company") driven by [Montague Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montague_Roberts "Montague Roberts"), one of the drivers for the team who had won the [1908 New York to Paris Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_New_York_to_Paris_Race "1908 New York to Paris Race") in that car.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908a-19)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-21) Montague had also competed in a 1907 24-hour race held at Morris Park when it was used for automobile racing.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-22) Previous launch attempts on the day of the exhibition had used a tow horse; out of six tries, only two got off the ground, reaching an altitude of about 20 feet (6.1 m).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-23) Lesh had also planned to show a large [box kite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_kite "Box kite") that day.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-24)

[![Image 6: A man wearing a white shirt, tie, and cap sits on a three-wheeled vehicle. The wheels appear to be from a bicycle. In the rear is some machinery and a large propeller. The man is holding in one hand what appears to be a tiller for steering the front wheel, and in the other controls for the machinery.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png/250px-Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Glenn_Curtiss_Seated_on_a_Wind_Wagon.png)

Glenn Curtiss on a wind wagon (date and location unknown)

The exhibition included a wind wagon contest, these being wheeled ground vehicles driven by propeller thrust.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16)_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ described one of these as resembling "a huge tricycle with a propeller eight feet long in front and a gasoline motor behind".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-25) Inventors scheduled to show their wagons included astronomer [William Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Pickering "William Henry Pickering"), aviation pioneer [Glenn Curtiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Curtiss "Glenn Curtiss"), W. A. Custard,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-The_New_York_Times_1908c-16) and [Julian P. Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_P._Thomas "Julian P. Thomas").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:19-26) According to Curtiss, the purpose of the wind wagon was to test the power of motors and the efficiency of propellers[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-27) and it had no commercial value.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-28)

Thomas's machine was wrecked two days before the exhibition, when he crashed during a practice run while trying to avoid a motorcycle. About 40 motorcyclists were using the track to prepare for a race scheduled to be held on exhibition day; Thomas believed they had already cleared the track and entered the course, running at high speed. He sustained severe injuries which were initially thought to have been fatal, but after several minutes of [unconsciousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconsciousness "Unconsciousness"), he opened his eyes, asked for a [cigarette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cigarette "Cigarette"), and refused to be taken to a hospital. Recuperating at home, Thomas asked that the machine be repaired so another driver could use it during the exhibition.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:19-26)

Two weeks after the 1908 exhibition, Lee Burridge spoke at the November 2 annual meeting of the Aero Club, reflecting on the schism which led to the founding of the Aeronautical Society. He complained of the "apathy of the Aero Club" when, after he had identified Morris Park as a potential site, they failed to act on the opportunity. [Augustus Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Post "Augustus Post"), secretary of the Aero Club, replied that doing so would have split the membership into two classes, to which he was opposed. Post added that the club was still seeking to "secure extensive grounds for motor ballooning and aeroplaning, with [hydrogen gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifting_gas#Hydrogen "Lifting gas") facilities, [machine shops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_shop "Machine shop"), and suitable buildings for storage, within easy distance of the city".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:23-29)

Members of the opposition group who had split off to form the new society acknowledged that while Morris Park was too small, it would serve a temporary function while they continued to search for a larger facility. A motion authorizing the Aero Club to work together with the Aeronautical Society to jointly search for a location was discussed, but failed.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:23-29)

The Golden Flyer at Morris Park, 1909

A second annual exhibition was held on June 26, 1909, with 2000 people in attendance[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30) on a day with ideal flying weather[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) but with near-record high temperatures.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32) The low attendance left the Society with a $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024) deficit.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32)

The highlight of the event was a series of flights by Curtiss in a [biplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biplane "Biplane") named the _[Golden Flyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss\_No.\_1 "Curtiss No. 1")_ which the Society had purchased from Curtiss and his partner [Augustus Herring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Moore_Herring "Augustus Moore Herring") for $5,000.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:11-33) This set a number of records; the flights themselves were the first airplane flights ever taken over New York City,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-34) the purchase was the first to a civilian owner, and the [Herring-Curtiss Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss_Aeroplane_and_Motor_Company "Curtiss Aeroplane and Motor Company") was the first aeroplane manufacturing company in the country.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:11-33) The terms of the sale included training for two pilots (Charles Willard and Alexander Williams[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-35)), and an obligation for Curtiss to fly it the exhibition. The Curtiss design used [ailerons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aileron "Aileron") for [roll control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_flight_control_system "Aircraft flight control system") instead of the [wing warping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_warping "Wing warping") system employed by the [Wright Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers "Wright brothers"), making the airplane more stable and more maneuverable.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-36)

> "That the defendant, alleging to be formed for the purpose of promoting aerial flying, procured the Herring-Curtiss Company and one Glenn H. Curtiss, personally, both of Hammondsport, N.Y., to make the flying machines herin complained of and deliver them to the defendant, under whose auspices the said Glenn H. Curtiss is giving public exhibition flights with the said infringing flying machines within the jurisdiction of this court; that the defendant has purchased such machines from one or both of said parties, and has charged the public for admission to said exhibition flights, receiving large sums in gate, or ticket, money."

Quote from Wright Brothers patent suit

The flight of the Golden Flyer created legal controversy when two months later the Wright Brothers filed a [patent infringement suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") against the Aeronautic Society in the [United States Circuit Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_circuit_court "United States circuit court"), claiming infringement of their 1906 patent. The suit ([one of many](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wright_brothers_patent_war "Wright brothers patent war") the Wrights would eventually file against competitors) demanded that the Society be permanently [injuncted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunction "Injunction") from further infringement, disclose how much money had been made from the exhibitions, and turn over for destruction all "machinery, flying machines, and parts thereof" which infringed the patents.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-37)

The first flight was a straight-line flight covering 300 yards (270 m), averaging 30 feet (9.1 m) in altitude. _[The Brooklyn Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn\_Eagle "Brooklyn Eagle")_ noted that "his adjustment of his controls to uneven wind currents was absolutely accurate".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) The remainder of the flights took place after twilight, having been delayed by puffy winds, with the event being forced to conclude as darkness fell. The rough ground at the field was a complicating factor, making landings difficult.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:5-38) One flight lasted 1 minute 45 2/5 seconds, completing either three-quarters or a full lap (sources differ) around the 1-mile (1.6 km) track at an altitude of 20 feet (6.1 m), flying between trees along the [backstretch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backstretch "Backstretch") and sometimes reaching as high as 60 feet (18 m). The aircraft was reported as "always under perfect control".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) This flight was the first time Curtiss had completed a flight around a circular course, although [Henri Farman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Farman "Henri Farman") and the Wright Brothers had both already accomplished this feat.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-39) Curtiss had hesitated before making the turn at the north end of the track, which had been criticized as being too confining.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:14-32)

It is banked at approximately 45 degrees.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png/250px-William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_Martin_Glider_at_Morris_Park_1909.png)

William Martin's glider at Morris Park

William H. Martin flew a glider towed by an automobile driven by his wife. He had only gone about 50 yards (46 m) when the tow rope broke and the glider crashed; he suffered minor injuries but the aircraft was severely damaged.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:1-30) The safety of the craft was demonstrated on September 21 when Martin's eight-year-old granddaughter, Blanche, made several solo flights, becoming the youngest person to make a flight in a heavier-than-air craft.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:4-40)

Martin's glider had originally been constructed on his farm in [Canton, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton,_Ohio "Canton, Ohio"), equipped with sled runners for operation on snow. The V-shaped lower wings added stability as a result of the [dihedral effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dihedral_(aeronautics) "Dihedral (aeronautics)"). It first flew on January 12, 1909, launched from the top of a hill and towed by Martin's horse named Old Billy. The first flight covered 200 feet (61 m) reaching a maximum altitude of 25 feet (7.6 m). Over the next few days, over 100 flights were conducted, with Martin's wife, son, and pet dog all taking turns. Martin brought the glider to Morris Park in May 1909, where it continued to make demonstration flights, being pulled around the track at 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) behind an automobile with a 150 ft (46 m) tow rope, and reaching altitudes as high as 75 feet (23 m). By this time, the snow runners had been replaced with wheels.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:4-40)

The UK-based [Flight Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_International "Flight International") called the Martin glider demonstration the most notable event of the day, after Curtiss's flight. They took a negative view, however, of Martin's craft, calling it an "example of the foolhardiness of tests of this character" and writing that "there is little or nothing to be learned through being towed behind a car in this manner ... the conditions do not represent the problems of flight in the least". They described the flight as a "short and erratic aerial journey". They noted that the presence of the tow rope restricted operation the aircraft and negatively affected its stability.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-41)

### Additional exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Additional exhibits")]

Frederick Schneider demonstrated a motor-driven [catapult-assisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_catapult "Aircraft catapult") airplane of his own construction, named _The Brooklyn_. The craft failed to get off the ground due to a rusty launching rail and too little weight loaded into the catapult, only managing to slide along the grass for 100 feet (30 m). There were also [parachute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute "Parachute") jumps from [hot air balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_air_balloon "Hot air balloon"), with Paul Bloomfield jumping from 1,000 feet (300 m), and Mary Hunter from an altitude reported only as "far higher" than Bloomfield's.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:2-31) One of the less serious events was a "balloonatic race". This consisted of a person attempting to run while being supported by a lighter-than-air balloon with just enough buoyancy to support the person's weight.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:5-38)

In attendance at the 1908 exhibition was painter [Rudolph Dirks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Dirks "Rudolph Dirks"), better known as the cartoonist who drew _[The Katzenjammer Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Katzenjammer\_Kids "The Katzenjammer Kids")_. ### Frederick Schneider

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Frederick Schneider")]

In December 1908, a new airplane arrived at Morris Park: a biplane under construction by Frederick Schneider,[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-51) who had begun construction at his home in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), disassembled it there, delivered it to Morris Park on Christmas day, and had it reassembled by the 29th of December. The plane had a 30-foot (9.1 m) wingspan and with a pilot aboard weighed 630 pounds (290 kg) with a main wing loading of 1.7 pounds per square foot (8.3 kg/m 2). A 36 horsepower (27 kW) five-cylinder air-cooled engine drove three adjustable-pitch propellers.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-Aeronautics_1909b-47)

### Stanley Beach and Charles Willard

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Morris_Park_Aerodrome&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Stanley Beach and Charles Willard")]

[![Image 12: Head-on photograph of a monoplane. A man stands to the side of one wingtip.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Beach-Willard_Monoplane%2C_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg/250px-Beach-Willard_Monoplane%2C_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beach-Willard_Monoplane,_Charles_F._Willard_and_Stanley_Yale_Beach1.jpg)

Beach-Willard Monoplane

Stanley Beach and [Charles Willard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_F._Willard "Charles F. Willard") constructed a [monoplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoplane "Monoplane") at Morris Park patterned after those built by [Bleriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Bl%C3%A9riot "Louis Blériot") and [Antoinette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoinette_(manufacturer) "Antoinette (manufacturer)").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:21-52) Completed on May 31, 1909, it was reported to be the first monoplane flown in the United States. Beach claimed it was faster than either the Wright or Curtiss airplanes, and just as stable. He intended to show it at the Hudson-Fulton Celebration, and fly it from New York to [Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_New_York "Albany, New York").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-53)

The aeroplane had a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four-cylinder [water cooled engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cooling "Water cooling") and a [wing loading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wing_loading "Wing loading") of 2-1/2 lbs per square foot.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-54) The engine ran at 1000 RPM, driving a nine foot propeller at 500 RPM via a [chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") via a 2:1 reduction [sprocket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprocket "Sprocket").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-53) During early testing, the propeller turning at 300 RPM developed 325 pounds (147 kg) of [thrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust "Thrust").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-55) A July 1909 report in _Aeronautics_ gives a wingspan of 38 ft (11.6 m) and a weight of 750 pounds (340 kg) including the pilot.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:21-52) A newspaper report in October, however, said it had a 41 ft (12.5 m) wingspan, weighed 1,100 pounds (500 kg) without the pilot, and was equipped with inflatable [pontoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Float_(nautical) "Float (nautical)") for water landings.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:20-53)

In July 1908, 24-year-old Henry W. Walden, a New York City dentist and aviation enthusiast, read about the Aeronautics Society. He joined in September of that year and began designing and building aeroplanes at Morris Park, despite a lack of training in aerodynamics. His first design, a [tandem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tandem "Tandem") biplane called the _Walden I_, was predicated on his belief that earlier designs lacked sufficient wing area. Ready for flight testing in early spring 1909, it used an automobile engine supplied to him by the Society. The 15 horsepower (11 kW) 500 lb (230 kg) engine proved unsuitable and he abandoned the design. His second effort, the _Walden II_, was completed in late May. This also failed to get off the ground. Walden attributed the failure to insufficient wing area and extended the wingsan by 2 feet (0.61 m) on each side, but it was destroyed in a windstorm before another attempt at flight could be undertaken.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:22-56)

Encouraged by watching Glenn Curtiss's flights at the June 1909 exhibition, Walden began work on the _Walden III,_ which he decided needed to be smaller and less complicated than his previous two. He designed a monoplane, purchasing a [three cylinder Anzani engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzani_3-cylinder_fan_engines "Anzani 3-cylinder fan engines") capable of producing 25–30 horsepower (19–22 kW). The wing was designed in a way which made it possible to add additional panels to increase the wing area if needed. To expedite construction, Walden hired two assistants to work on the plane, and another dentist to take over most of his practice. The plane was completed in late November, but by that time the Society's lease was running out and the plane was moved to [another field in Mineola, Long Island,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)") where it was first test-flown on December 9.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:22-56)

American Eagle at Morris Park, 1909

In February 1908, aviator [Joel T. Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joel_T._Rice&action=edit&redlink=1 "Joel T. Rice (page does not exist)") (with financial backing from [John Andrew Riggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Andrew_Riggs "John Andrew Riggs")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:6-57)) formed the [Hot Springs Airship Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs_Airship_Company "Hot Springs Airship Company") in [Hot Springs, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs,_Arkansas "Hot Springs, Arkansas") whereupon they started work on a [dirigible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airship "Airship"), over 50-foot (15 m) long, named _The Arkansas Traveler._[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-58) In 1909, they moved the ship to New York, where they showed it at the [Hudson–Fulton Celebration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson%E2%80%93Fulton_Celebration "Hudson–Fulton Celebration"). They also began work at Morris Park on a larger ship, _The American Eagle,_ costing over $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024). At the time, this was the largest steel-framed airship in the country.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:6-57) The name was unpopular with New Yorkers, leading to the newspapers of the time referring to it as _The Arkansas Traveler_, the same name as the previous ship.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:7-59) Plans were being made for the [Seeing New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seeing_New_York "Seeing New York") company to use the ship for sightseeing tours over New York City.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-60)

_The American Eagle_ had a 100-foot (30 m) envelope holding 33,000 cubic feet (930 m 3) of gas with an 80-foot (24 m) compartment providing seating for 15 passengers.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:15-61) Instead of the usual rudder, she had a large propeller mounted so that in addition to providing propulsive thrust, it could [pivot left and right providing lateral control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrust_vectoring "Thrust vectoring"), Two smaller propellers could be pivoted up and down for vertical control, a system which Rice had patented in 1904. The ship included a system which captured and reused hydrogen gas that leaked from the envelope.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:16-62)

The ship was intended to be used for cross-country flights, with the initial trip scheduled from New York to [Washington DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."). Stops along the way were planned at 50–75-mile (80–121 km) intervals to show off the ship. Riggs said that the trip was intended "to demonstrate the practical uses of a properly equipped dirigible balloon for long-continued cross-country travel".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:16-62) Unfortunately, the flight never happened. Immediately after being launched, the horizontal planes accidentally hit the propellers, destroying them, making it impossible to control the ship. A gale-force storm two days later caused irreparable damage to the gas envelope.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:7-59)

Morris Park proved to be too small to serve the needs of the Aeronautical Society. After surveying the available locations near New York City, Glenn Curtiss recommended moving to the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome (later renamed [Roosevelt Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_Field_(airport) "Roosevelt Field (airport)")), near [Mineola, Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineola,_New_York "Mineola, New York").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-63) On May 9 (another source says April 10[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:12-64)) 1910, a wind-blown fire destroyed the Morris Park property. The [Van Nest Hose Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Nest_Hose_Company "Van Nest Hose Company") responded, stopping trains on the [New Haven Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") for several hours because they needed to lay their hoses across the rails. Despite their efforts, the fire burned all afternoon consuming the race track and several nearby buildings.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:13-8) The property was later subdivided into building lots.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-:12-64)

In the 1920s, there were efforts to create a new airport about 2 miles (3.2 km) to the northeast, in a marshy area near the [Hutchinson River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutchinson_River "Hutchinson River"), which was later the site of [Freedomland U.S.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedomland_U.S.A. "Freedomland U.S.A.") and, still later, of [Co-op City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Co-op_City,_Bronx "Co-op City, Bronx"). The Bronx Chamber of Commerce made one failed attempt in 1927. Another attempt in 1929 by [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") failed when the [stock market crashed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_crash_of_1929 "Wall Street crash of 1929").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Park_Aerodrome#cite_note-66)

Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history
===========================================================

By Ben Kochman Posted on [June 10, 2014](https://www.bxtimes.com/archivist-hopes-morris-park-will-honor-its-aviation-history/)

![Image 9: Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history](https://www.bxtimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/21-airport-2014-05-22-bx01_z.jpg?quality=51&w=500)

Photo by Ben Kochman||

The old Morris park racetrack is famous – but how about some love for the Morris Park Aerodrome?

A local historian hopes his efforts to recognize his hometown’s unique aviation past will get off the ground.

Morris Park is well known for its namesake racetrack, which hosted the Belmont Stakes from the mid-19th century until 1904. But an archivist at Fordham Prep has tracked down evidence that the east Bronx neighborhood was once also home to some of the world’s first glimpses of flying machines.

**First helicopter flight**

“There’s very little of Morris Park history that we celebrate and put out on public display, “ said Louis DiGiorno, who came across his nabe’s aviation past while researching Fordham Prep alumni, many of whom were pilots. “With something this important, we should think about marking it.”

In 1908, the New York Aeronautical Society rented out the former Morris Park racetrack and invited some of the world’s aviation inventors – including the creator of the helicopter – to try out their flying machines at the site.

“Wilbur H. Kimbull’s heliocopter, upon which he has been working for several years, is being assembled at Morris Park and by the end of the week he expects to be ready to try the ascensional power of the machine,” read a story in the September 7, 1908 New York Times.

The airplanes that made it into the air did not go far. The show’s organizers removed the fences around the old racetrack to create an “unobstructed straightway for a flight of at least one kilometer,” according to the Times.

Some of the machines were able to take off — others just looked very impressive.

“The airplane that won design for best airplane couldn’t even fly,” said borough historian Lloyd Ultan.

**Proposed plaque**

The racetrack burned down a few years later, said Ultan, before the land was auctioned off in 1913 to residential real estate developers.

DiGiorno has proposed a plaque or flag in recognition of the area’s aviation history to Community Board 11.

He’s even got a neighborhood tagline ready:

“Morris park: looking up since 1908.”

A Brief History of the First flying club and Civil airport
----------------------------------------------------------

### By Willie Bodenstein

**Willie Bodenstein
10.03.2024

![Image 1: Black and white scene shows many people gathered on a field with tents and a raised structure behind them](https://pilotspost.co.za/articles/240309ABriefHistoryoftheFirstflyingclubandCivilairport/01.jpg)**

**Morris Park in New York City was a well-known horse racing track during the 1800 and early 1900. The track eventually fell into disuse and 1908 the Aeronautical Society who had obtained a lease on the property rented out the former racetrack and invited some of the world's aviation inventors - including the creator of the helicopter - to try out their flying machines at the site. [![Image 2: Air rescue team prepares for an air rescue mission in front of their helicopter](http://pilotspost.com/add/DJA202308List.jpg)](http://pilotspost.com/PsPpyRedB0125 "Click here for more information")[![Image 3: Yellow Cubby Mk II airplane](http://pilotspost.com/add/Cubby202002List.jpg)](http://pilotspost.com/PsPpyRedB0132 "Click here for more information")

 The fences around the old racetrack were removed to create an unobstructed straightway for a flight of at least one kilometre. The largest dirigible in history to that time at a full 105 feet in length, was built there, and one of the first gliders, piloted by 17-year-old Lawrence Lesh, was launched from the former track that year.[![Image 4: Avionics without limits saving weight, space and money with Kanardia, Nesis, PFD, auto pilot, engine monitors, digital instruments, TO, KTX2-S MODE-S, KTX2-F STACK, KRT2-S VHF-COM, KRT2-F STACK, NEX-NAV ADS-B, f.u.n.k.e. Avionics GmbH, ATR 833S VHF COM, TRT 800 H LCD MODE-S, ATR 833 OLED VHF COM, ATR 833 LCD VHF COM, TM 250 TRAFFIC and PJ Aviation land, sea and air](http://pilotspost.com/add/PJAviationGen.jpg)](http://pilotspost.com/PsPpyRedB0150 "Click here for more information")

 Wilbur H. Kimbull's helicopter, upon which he has been working for several years, was also assembled at Morris Park. Some of the machines were able to take off - others just looked very impressive. An airplane that won design for best airplane hosted at the field couldn't even fly, others made it into the air did not go far.

6.title: Morris Park - The Bronx
6.content:
[![Image 1: New York City map with the Bronx highlighted in gold](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ngoF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b0f580b-2c96-4cef-87b9-e2a2d1d1e36d_1270x1272.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ngoF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b0f580b-2c96-4cef-87b9-e2a2d1d1e36d_1270x1272.jpeg)

Before I started researching Morris Park, I assumed it got its name from the Morris family, the namesake of the neighborhoods of [Port Morris](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/port-morris-the-bronx) and Morrasania, also in the Bronx. However, the neighborhood is actually named in honor of horse enthusiast and “Lottery King” John Albert Morris.

[![Image 2: Neon sign for Window King above a phone number](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUJN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9296720-0730-4733-b2ce-b1b0ec97b46f_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GUJN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9296720-0730-4733-b2ce-b1b0ec97b46f_2000x1600.jpeg)

Morris Park is between Pelham Parkway to the North, the Hutchinson River Parkway to the East, the Amtrak Northeast Corridor tracks to the south, and White Plains Road to the West. The neighborhood has traditionally been Italian American, though there has been a significant increase in the Albanian population in recent years.

[![Image 3: Map of Morris Park, Bronx, outlined in orange](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uMYE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde598ce8-768a-418e-a081-8ea0526986f2_990x818.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uMYE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde598ce8-768a-418e-a081-8ea0526986f2_990x818.jpeg)

John Morris made his fortune from the Louisiana State Lottery Company, a venture he founded in 1868 under the pretext of raising money to fund reconstruction efforts after the Civil War.

At the time, most states had banned lotteries since they were, at best, immoral and, at worst, brazenly corrupt. For a long time, The Louisiana State Lottery Company was the only legal lottery in the US, a distinction it earned through generous bribes and influence peddling. Taking advantage of the reach of the U.S. Postal Service, the company sold lottery tickets nationwide, earning it the nickname of the Golden Octopus. It quickly became one of the largest businesses in the United States.

[![Image 4: The Lottery Octopus cartoon by Puck showing the tentacles of a lottery octopus reaching out from the South into other parts of the country](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xXfq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ad54431-4f95-4566-9e53-37bfb1b7ac2b_616x368.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xXfq!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ad54431-4f95-4566-9e53-37bfb1b7ac2b_616x368.jpeg)

At its peak, the lottery was generating $2,000,000 in sales per week, a ”fountain of wealth to which that of Monte Cristo was but a mere bagatelle.” [1](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-1-140966467)

Finally, in 1890, Congress outlawed the mailing of any lottery-related material. Morris moved his headquarters to Honduras and rebranded as The Honduras Lottery Company. He circumvented the new postal ban by having employees collect and carry lottery tickets in their luggage. The scheme continued to operate in the shadows until 1907, when two printing presses owned by the company in Alabama and Delaware were seized, and they were forced to dissolve.

In 1889, flush with lottery money, Morris opened the Morris Park Racecourse, once described as "the finest race track in the world,” on the site of present-day Morris Park. From 1890 to 1904, the racecourse hosted the Belmont Stakes.

[![Image 5: Clubhouse with an additional building in vintage tones](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aKNp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b95fb57-c071-459c-95ca-0d5439eb4b0e_1916x1096.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!aKNp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9b95fb57-c071-459c-95ca-0d5439eb4b0e_1916x1096.jpeg)

Maybe this haunted looking clubhouse kept people away

The Belmont was originally held at the Jerome racetrack, which I wrote about in my [Kingsbridge Heights](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/bones-of-the-buddha-in-the-bronx) post.

[![Image 6: Crowds of people and carriages waiting to get into Morris Park Race track](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ekKz!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40bd38b4-5fe7-4607-97d1-abab41ead77c_2060x707.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ekKz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40bd38b4-5fe7-4607-97d1-abab41ead77c_2060x707.jpeg)

Morris Park Race Track, the entrance to grandstand, B.J., Falk, 1903 

The race track closed in 1904 due to declining attendance and, for a couple of years, was repurposed for automobiles, with the first-ever Indy car race held there in 1905.

Then, in 1908, the Aeronautic Society secured the lease for the 372-acre site in the Bronx, paving the way for the world’s first formal airfield.

The Aeronautic Society of New York was formed by members of The Aero Club of America, who were frustrated by the latter’s single-minded focus on hot-air ballooning. They viewed the Aero club as “dominated by a handful of elite sportsmen who had taken up ballooning, supplemented by a larger number of armchair aeronauts drawn from the cream of New York society.”[2](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-2-140966467)

The Aeronautic Society members wanted to focus on "heavier-than-air flight,” inspired no doubt by the well-documented successes of the Wright Brothers.

Society members set up shop in the vacant stables and barns and began to build some of the most fantastical machines ever seen.

> **Soon, the people of the neighborhood began to whisper to one another that queer-looking machines were being built up at the racetrack, and every day, curious, inquisitive little throngs would venture in and peep. Never before had the like of such things been seen in New York City!**[3](https://theneighborhoods.substack.com/p/morris-park-the-bronx#footnote-3-140966467)

Take, for example, William Kimball’s helicopter with its 20 rotors driven by an intricate system of leather belts and pulleys.

[![Image 7: A man standing in a very complex machine covered with small propellers](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m9kk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8caf17bf-64ef-4605-83d5-90b1a9d1b649_1666x1255.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m9kk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8caf17bf-64ef-4605-83d5-90b1a9d1b649_1666x1255.png)

[![Image 8: L'Eole, or Bat, designed by Clement Ader, is an early flying machine with multiple propellers arranged on a frame](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GcOx!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F213e3d8e-662a-436c-9cec-af9097bd41ef_548x301.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GcOx!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F213e3d8e-662a-436c-9cec-af9097bd41ef_548x301.jpeg)

Not to be outdone was the Rickman Helicopter, boasting 32 propellors powered by two men, possessing what must have been enormous quads, astride a tandem bicycle.

[![Image 9: The multi-seat bicycle equipped with a large umbrella-like canopy, surrounded by a group of people in formal attire](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qzgC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb1e3288-171b-43d7-abf1-c9492be83ae1_1024x532.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qzgC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb1e3288-171b-43d7-abf1-c9492be83ae1_1024x532.jpeg)

And there was the C.W. Williams’ “weird and wonderful ” monoplane

[![Image 10: The Ader Éole, a bat-like aircraft of 1890, stands on a grassy field surrounded by a crowd of onlookers in a historical black and white photo](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!R77L!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6b01372-0c72-40a1-bc13-10590622b057_1000x628.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!R77L!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6b01372-0c72-40a1-bc13-10590622b057_1000x628.jpeg)

On November 3rd, 1908, those inventions and dozens more were put to the test in front of a crowd of 20,000 spectators. Not a single one of them managed to get off the ground.

At least the wind-powered gliders made it airborne, though, in Lawrence Lesh’s case, he may have been better off staying put. Lesh spent seven months recovering in nearby Fordam Hospital after the crowds, excited to finally have a reason to look up, encroached upon his landing spot, forcing him into a crash landing that broke his ankle.

[![Image 11: Laurence Lesh in his flying machine, over Morris-Park, New York in 1909, according to the vintage postcard](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1es5!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40941b03-a58b-46a6-af98-e0f0d5c01915_364x580.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1es5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40941b03-a58b-46a6-af98-e0f0d5c01915_364x580.jpeg)

“There is an art, it says, or rather, a knack to flying. The knack lies in learning how to throw yourself at the ground and miss. … Clearly, it is this second part, the missing, which presents the difficulties.” - Douglas Adams

These pictures reminded me more than a bit of the work of Shana and Robert ParkeHarrison. In particular, this image, The Sower:

[![Image 12: A man pours material from a box on a swing attached to a fantastical machine with propellers over a field](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EEyr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb9a20f8-cf88-4e8c-b504-7883277b1868_505x600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EEyr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Feb9a20f8-cf88-4e8c-b504-7883277b1868_505x600.jpeg)

After a big fire at the racetrack in 1910, the city auctioned off the land to real estate developers in 1913.

[![Image 13: Vintage real estate advertisement for the auction sale of 3019 lots at Morris Park Race Track in the Bronx borough of New York City, starting Saturday, May 31, 1913](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZsQU!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61bdfe91-4322-4962-a17b-cd9ddcac162c_1242x939.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZsQU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F61bdfe91-4322-4962-a17b-cd9ddcac162c_1242x939.jpeg)

Several years ago, while working with the great musician and photographer [John Cohen](https://www.johncohenworks.com/) on his archive in the Hudson Valley, I would frequently drive by the blunt silhouette of a building slowly rising on the edge of the Hutchinson River Parkway. One day, I finally pulled over to take a picture.

[![Image 14: An off-angle view of a large, light grey, building with long, thin rectangular windows](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p7Y!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd12b3467-da97-4c21-b142-e2649ff1cf7a_1599x2000.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1p7Y!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd12b3467-da97-4c21-b142-e2649ff1cf7a_1599x2000.jpeg)

I love unadorned buildings, structures reduced to the simplest of geometric forms. While I can appreciate the haphazard offset stacks of [56 Leonard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/56_Leonard_Street) (the Jenga building) or the graceful concrete curves of Eero Saarinen’s TWA terminal, there is just something about a simple rectangle that feels both ancient and futuristic.

PSAC II, a 450,000-square-foot monolith, is a perfect cube, a 240-foot wide by 240-foot tall concrete block sheathed in a serrated aluminum facade. The near absence of windows is a security measure.

PSAC stands for Public Safety Answering Center. It can handle all emergency 911 calls and communications in the event that PSAC I (in the Metrotech Center in downtown Brooklyn) goes down. The building was designed to survive a natural disaster or an attack and is said to be “virtually impregnable.” Anti-ram walls and bollards surround the grounds,and the loading bays are equipped with blast doors. There are multiple generators and battery systems, along with enough food to keep the center running for days off the grid. It is a fortress.

[![Image 15: A tall building with a square design sits behind a variety of trees and grass](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NHlM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff69888ff-0000-4578-bb5c-9ae1ffd3dc4c_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NHlM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff69888ff-0000-4578-bb5c-9ae1ffd3dc4c_2000x1600.jpeg)

The Morris Park Crew, or MPC, was a gang of graffiti “bombers” formed in the neighborhood in 1977. In the early 80s, notorious bomber Cap One took over the crew. Cap was infamous for “going over” other graffiti artists’ work, a practice that made him the public enemy of anybody not in the MPC.

[![Image 16: Bridge in a city features graffiti and other paint on its supporting wall](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EQns!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff04c36e4-5fd8-47fa-9f73-5f25209f02e3_2000x1600.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!EQns!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff04c36e4-5fd8-47fa-9f73-5f25209f02e3_2000x1600.jpeg)

Not MPC’s work

The fantastic 1983 documentary [Style Wars](https://youtu.be/qqUwNkr-B3k?si=fao-ItZGosdDxFQT) (free on Youtube) was called the “defining documentary of early hip-hop culture" by Pitchfork (RIP). The doc features interviews with graffiti writers like Cap, Kase 2, and Skeme, whose interview alongside his mothers is one of the best parts of the film.

Other highlights include footage of the dance battle between the Rock Steady Crew and the Dynamic Rockers and a clip of Mayor Ed Koch half-seriously proposing that wolves patrol the train yards to deter would-be vandals. There is no better document of early 80s New York City culture.

**5/5** stars

Here is another photograph from the great [Camilo Jose Vergara](https://www.camilojosevergara.com/). Vergara came to the US in the 1960s from Chile to study sociology at Notre Dame University in the 1960s and has been documenting the urban condition ever since.

[![Image 35: Person sitting on a bench in a subway station on 180th Street](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ud2C!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a454709-2114-4449-ac6f-b40cb9f3f7a3_1024x685.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ud2C!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a454709-2114-4449-ac6f-b40cb9f3f7a3_1024x685.jpeg)

180th St. Station, Morris Park Ave., South Bronx, 1983

[![Image 36: Painting of a historic scene showing airplanes and people together](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IZth!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0bf81517-6cf5-4178-83c0-7ab969167320_2315x641.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IZth!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0bf81517-6cf5-4178-83c0-7ab969167320_2315x641.jpeg)

*   This painting, _[The Fledglings](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.smithsonianmag.com%2Fair-space-magazine%2Fthe-katzenjammer-kids-take-to-the-air-120519321%2F&psig=AOvVaw2b9KYnMwfevilCzDhq0ujW&ust=1706221552954000&source=images&cd=vfe&opi=89978449&ved=0CBUQjhxqFwoTCKD\_s9-I94MDFQAAAAAdAAAAABAE)_[by Rudolph Dirks](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.smithsonianmag.com%2Fair-space-magazine%2Fthe-katzenjammer-kids-take-to-the-air-120519321%2F&psig=AOvVaw2b9KYnMwfevilCzDhq0ujW&ust=1706221552954000&source=images&cd=vfe&opi=89978449&ved=0CBUQjhxqFwoTCKD_s9-I94MDFQAAAAAdAAAAABAE), depicts that first exhibition at the Morris Park Aerodrome in 1908. Dirks was the cartoonist behind the Katzenjammer Kids, the longest running newspaper comic in history.

*   Jake “Raging Bull” LaMotta lived in Morris Park. Can you find him in this picture taken outside his home?

[![Image 37: A crowd of people in black and white are gathered outside a house to welcome Jake LaMotta, with signs that say Welcome Home](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vqj3!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4dcdd266-960d-48bd-80c8-3bde24ad5f97_1050x857.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vqj3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4dcdd266-960d-48bd-80c8-3bde24ad5f97_1050x857.jpeg) 
*   I stumbled upon this [game simulation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ej8eqbYAjxg&embeds_referring_euri=https%3A%2F%2Ftheneighborhoods.substack.com%2F&feature=emb_imp_woyt&themeRefresh=1) someone made of a race on the Old Morris Park racetrack. Amazing!

*   [Conti’s Pastry Shoppe](https://contispastryshoppe.com/)is an old-school Italian bakery that has been in business since 1921. The restored bakery has tin ceilings and wooden cases filled with a Thiebaudian display of treats.

[![Image 38: Display case filled with an assortment of cakes and pastries, including chocolate, carrot cake, red velvet, Napoleons, and cream pastries](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kweg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5e49a3c5-d10b-40b1-a4c9-533a51386953_1600x2000.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Kweg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5e49a3c5-d10b-40b1-a4c9-533a51386953_1600x2000.jpeg)

[![Image 39: Honduras Lottery Co. | Contemporary Evening Auction | 2023 | Sotheby's](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!za0K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fff51a8aa-e566-4381-a33e-cf86e8cadc94_385x388.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!za0K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fff51a8aa-e566-4381-a33e-cf86e8cadc94_385x388.jpeg)

*   This is Frank Stella’s piece, **Honduras Lottery Co.** It sold last year for 18.7 million dollars. I couldn’t find any reason why Stella named the piece after John Albert Morris’ lottery scheme, but I do think had Morris been aware of the pricing of the contemporary art market, he might have decided to become an artist rather than a Lottery King. Or as “The Guy” on Twitter says:

[![Image 40: The Guy's tweet, dated Nov 16, 2023, criticizes the art world in terms of money laundering and comparing the art to turds in the toilet made by Picasso](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lWdI!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F699afa41-ff1d-4e66-ac7c-e59f29391431_1206x298.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lWdI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F699afa41-ff1d-4e66-ac7c-e59f29391431_1206x298.jpeg)

Decades before The Bronx neighborhood of Morris Park came to be, it was home to the 360 acre Morris Park Racecourse which ran from 1889 until 1904 as an important center of American thoroughbred horse racing which was the home of the Belmont Stakes from 1890 until 1904 and even saw the famous Preakness Stakes in 1890.

The 1 1/4 mile track was bounded by what is today Sacket Avenue, Williamsbridge Road, Bronxdale Avenue, and Pelham Parkway and by 1902 attendance was no longer what it once was and a decision was made to shut down the track which saw its last horse race on October 15, 1904.

8.title: Morris Field (L-118)
8.description: A U.S. Army air base, 1941-1946. Named for Maj. William Morris, WWI pilot. The 5,000 acre facility became airport at this site.
8.content:
[](https://www.dncr.nc.gov/blog/2024/01/17/morris-field-l-118)

**Location:**West Blvd. at Airport Dr., Charlotte

**County:**Mecklenburg

**Original Date Cast:**2021

Morris Field was a U.S. Army Air Corps base at Charlotte during World War II. It was one of nine military airfields in North Carolina during the conflict.

The airport began as a municipal airfield in the 1930s. Originally, Charlotte was served by a small, privately-owned airstrip known as the Charlotte Airport (later known as Cannon Field), which utilized the old airstrip constructed during World War I as part of the army base, Camp Greene. The postwar private airport provided only limited service, however, and Charlotte mayor Ben E. Douglas pushed for the creation of a municipal airfield. The city received funding for the construction of an airport by the Works Progress Administration in 1935. By mid-1937, the project was completed, and the facility was opened as the Charlotte Municipal Airport, with Eastern Airlines offering scheduled passenger service.

In April 1941, the airport was taken over by the U.S. Army Air Corps and was renamed the Charlotte Army Air Base. It was initially a small operation with only three runways. It served as a training facility for pilots and gunners and also as a center for maintenance and repair. Following the outbreak of World War II, the base was renamed in January 1942, this time as Morris Field, after Major William Colb Morris (1891-1939). A native of Harrisburg, N.C., Morris was a graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point and had served as a flight instructor and as a pilot during World War I.

During the war, Morris Field expanded in size with many new buildings added. The Army invested over $5 million in improvements to the facility, and the base proved to be a major boost to the local economy. Various units rotated in and out of the base for periods of duty lasting several months each. The base published its own newspaper and broadcast a weekly radio show. Some commercial aviation continued to operate from the north side of the airfield.

In 1946, the U.S. Army closed Morris Field and the airport reverted back to Charlotte, resuming its prewar name of the Charlotte Municipal Airport. Many of the wartime barracks and other military buildings were remodeled into apartments as the city faced a postwar housing shortage. In 1954, it was renamed Douglas Municipal Airport to honor the mayor who was responsible for the airport’s original creation, and it became Charlotte Douglas International Airport in 1982. It is still in operation today.
